newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's troubled Jinro to restructure.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's troubled Jinro to restructure.

text.p: South Korea's corporate nightmare deepened on Tuesday when the nation's 19th-largest conglomerate, the Jinro Group, announced it would sell off some business lines and other assets because of financial pressures.

Jinro, Korea's largest producer of distilled spirits, said in a statement it would raise a total of 1.2 trillion won ($1.34 billion) by the end of 1998 to bring its equity-to-assets ratio to 24.7 percent from the current 4.43 percent.
"We will sell our canned food and soft drink lines and other assets, including real estate, to improve our financial status," the statement said.

An official at the Commercial Bank of Korea, Jinro's prime creditor, said the bank would consider fresh loans to Jinro if the group presented an acceptable restructuring plan. He would not discuss details.
Domestic media earlier reported Jinro had asked the commercial bank to supply 200 billion won in rescue loans.
Jinro officials refused to comment on the group's efforts to seek new loans.
Analysts said the group had accumulated more than three trillion won in debts after unsuccessfully trying to expand into distribution, beer and construction.
"Jinro's problems are no better than those of Hanbo and Sammi," said Hwang Chang, an analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.
"But the government is unlikely to let Jinro go bankrupt because it cannot handle another corporate failure after the Hanbo loans scandal and Sammi Steel's failure rocked the nation."

The Hanbo loans-for-kickbacks scandal, which began with the collapse of group flagship Hanbo Steel Co in January under $5.8 billion in debts, revealed a web of corruption and influence-peddling involving top bankers and politicians.
Sammi Steel, flagship of the Sammi Group, failed in March because of heavy debt.
"Jinro's failure would deal a crushing blow to the already troubled economy," said Han Sang-choon, an analyst at Daewoo Research Institute.

"The government may have to bail out Jinro even if it defies the OECD rules," Han said. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, which Korea joined last year, frowns on government bailouts.
Analysts said President Kim Young-sam and his ruling New Korea Party would not want any major corporate bankruptcies in the run-up to December's presidential election.

Elsewhere, officials of the nation's commercial banks on Tuesday agreed in principle to provide assistance to companies experiencing cash-flow problems, as long as they were not facing imminent bankruptcy.
Financial institutions have become reluctant to give fresh loans to companies rumoured to be in trouble, leading to an increase in debt defaults among smaller companies.
Brokers said the effect of Jinro's troubles on the stock market was mixed. Stocks closed at 701.39, down 2.81 points.
"Jinro's move disclosed its financial problems. At the same time some investors believe the restructuring effort will improve its financial status," said Koh Kyong-bae of Hyundai Securities.
Jinro Ltd, the flagship spirits maker of the group's 22 companies, fell 800 won to its daily limit of 10,400.
